newsitem.title: UK: European bourses rebound from "grey Friday".
newsitem.headline: European bourses rebound from "grey Friday".

text.p: European bourses opened sharply higher on Monday and the dollar rallied in early trade as the markets decided Friday's global turmoil was overdone.

London, Paris and Frankfurt all started up more than one percent and the dollar was more than half a pfennig stronger as the European currency focus switched from the shaky U.S. stock and bonds markets of last week to intensifying negotiations over European monetary union.

Shares plunged in a worldwide selloff on Friday, badly shaken by U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan warning about "irrational exuberance" in asset markets. The dollar and bonds were also dragged down.

But a partial bounce back by Wall Street after Europe had closed on Friday sparked a recovery in Asian markets overnight and the recovering sentiment carried over into Europe. The Dow closed down just 55.16 points down at 6,381.94.
Last week's global market tumble left the FTSE 100 index down 88.2 points, or 2.2 percent, at 3,963.0 on Friday -- its biggest one-day loss in percentage terms since February 1994.

Despite trading some 40 points higher on Monday, analysts said sentiment had taken a severe knock and any gains were likely to be capped, particularly after renewed talk of an early election following the latest outbreak of tension in the ruling Conservative Party.
"There is every chance the market will try to go a bit better today but I doubt if it will make up all Friday's losses," said one senior equity salesman.
One main mover was EMI, up 14p at 13.45 pounds, despite a denial from the company that it was in merger talks with Seagram's MCA music unit.
In Frankfurt early screen trading saw German stocks recover almost 1.5 percent and the trend continued in floor trade where the DAX index rebounded more than 2.5 percent.
Traders said the market was relieved by the relatively limited losses on Wall Street on Friday, the recovery in Asia and the firmer dollar, which makes German exports more attractive.
It was a similar story in Paris where shares started with an almost one percent bounce following a 2.26 percent drop on Friday.

On the currency front the dollar rallied as the market focus moved to monetary union developments. German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac were meeting in Nuremberg on Monday ahead of the European Union summit in Dublin next weekend.
Kohl and Chirac are expected to agree a common stance going into the weekend EU summit, which is seen as crucial to the future of monetary union.
By 1000 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.5525 marks compared with 1.5465 late on Friday. Against the yen, it was at 113.20 compared with 112.95 late last week.

Bank of England governor Eddie George described the market response to the Greenspan speech as an overreaction, and U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Greenspan was merely raising a question about stock market levels.

Yet, while analysts and officials said the reaction to Greenspan's comments was exaggerated by year-end profit-taking, British analysts said the risks of a rate rise at the Fed's policy-making meeting on December 17 had risen, and that was boosting the dollar.
The dollar should also be supported by talk of a further trimming of the key German securities repurchase rate and a pan-European desire for a stronger dollar against European currencies, they said.
CURRENCIES AT 1000 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 113.20 yen and 1.5525 marks against 112.95 yen and 1.5465 marks in late Europe on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1000 GMT
The FTSE 100 index of leading British shares were 36 points higher at 3,999.
In Paris, the CAC-40 share index was up 19.57 at 2,260.48.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt was up 76.45 at 2,868.41.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold opened easier at $368.60 compared with its Friday close of $369.65 ounce. Silver was also easier at $4.76.
